newsitem.title: KAZAKHSTAN: Uighur exiles claim China "revenge" bus bombings.
newsitem.headline: Uighur exiles claim China "revenge" bus bombings.

text.p: Moslem Uighur nationalists claimed responsibility on Tuesday for a series of bus bombings last week in northwestern China and for a similar, previously unreported attack on Monday.
A Chinese government official in the restive region of Xinjiang denied there had been a new blast on Monday, however.

A prominent spokesman for Uighur exiles told Reuters in Almaty, capital of neighbouring Kazakhstan, that the acts were in reprisal for deaths and arrests during a Chinese clampdown on the separatist movement over the past month.
"We intend to continue our struggle," Mukhiddin Mukhlisi added, saying three exile groups had joined forces after police and army killed 127 Uighurs and arrested hundreds more.

An official in Urumqi, capital of Xinjiang province, said at the weekend that seven people had died and 60 were hurt in three time-bomb explosions on buses in the city on February 24, coinciding with funeral rites for Chinese leader Deng Xiaoping.

Mukhlisi said he did not know how many victims there were in the latest attack on Monday on a bus travelling to Urumqi from Yining, near the Kazakh border. The blast occurred some 120 km (75 miles) east of Yining, he said.
"The explosion in the bus near the town of Kuldji (Yining) ...was our act of revenge for the crimes of the Chinese authorities," Mukhlisi said.
However, a government official in Yining said by telephone: "It's peaceful here. There's been no untoward incident."
"There have been a lot rumours like this recently," he added. There was no new bomb attack."

A spokesman for Uighur exiles in Russia, Sargari Tarym, said last week in Moscow: "We think that, in general, Deng's death will bring a power struggle within the Chinese elite. If that happens, the independence movement in Turkestan will intensify."
Mukhlisi said Beijing had launched a "hundred days anti-separatist campaign" against Uighur nationalists who want to establish an independent "East Turkestan" homeland.
Longer-term, he said, China was pursuing a policy of bringing in ethnic Han Chinese immigrants to Xinjiang and giving them favourable treatment over the Turkic-speaking Uighurs.

In February a huge anti-Chinese riot by local Uighurs broke out Yining. Beijing said the riot had erupted after a Uighur criminal suspect resisted arrest. Uighur exiles said it was triggered by "China's colonial policy, genocide, mass influx of ethnic Han Chinese and social economic problems of the Uighurs".
Chinese officials said nine people were killed in the clashes. Uighur leaders said at least 80 people were killed.
The riot was one of the largest, most violent demonstrations for independence in Xinjiang since the 1949 communist takeover.
Officially some nine million Uighurs live in China but nationalists put the number at over 20 million.
As many as 300,000 Uighurs live in the former Soviet Union, to which many fled in the 1960s during a period of Han Chinese discrimination against ethnic minorities.
About 180,000 have settled in Kazakhstan.

Uighur exiles have complained that China has increased pressure on their kinsmen in Xinjiang since signing a wide-ranging frontier treaty with Russia, Kazakhstan and other former Soviet states in Central Asia.

Moscow has denied that the treaty obliges it to extradite Uighur activists to China and Kazakhstan, dominated by the Uighurs' fellow Turkic-speaking Kazakhs, said last month it would remain neutral between the separatists and Beijing.
